title: San Francisco against ten peer areas on the federal measures
question: On the measures the federal housing department collects from every area in the same form, how does San Francisco compare, and what does each federal grant dollar buy?
finding: In federal fiscal year 2024, 17% of people leaving San Francisco's shelters, transitional housing and rapid rehousing went to permanent housing (891 of 5,131), against a middle figure of 36% in ten peer areas: rank 11 of 11, where 1 is best. Its federal homelessness grant of $56.2 million works out at $63,047 for each such exit, against a peer middle of $16,182 (rank 11 of 11, 1 being the fewest dollars). Among people already in permanent housing, 97% stayed housed, against 96%. In 2019, before many more shelter programmes began entering records, San Francisco reported 46% (521 of 1,143).
how: The federal housing department's System Performance Measures file gives, for every homelessness planning area and year, the federal grant awarded, people in the data system, people who left shelter, transitional housing, safe havens or rapid rehousing, and how many of them went to permanent housing. San Francisco is compared with Los Angeles, San Diego, Oakland and Alameda County, San José and Santa Clara County, Sacramento, Seattle and King County, Portland and Multnomah County, Denver, Houston and New York City. The peer figure is the median of the ten.
limits: Each area reports its own figures to the federal government from its own data system, under shared rules; no outside body recounts them. The federal grant is a small part of what San Francisco spends, most of which is local money, so dollars per exit compare federal money only and say nothing about total cost. The share leaving for housing depends on which programmes enter records: San Francisco's count of people leaving rose several-fold after 2019 as shelters joined the system, which lowers the share without any change on the ground, so its series is not comparable across that break. Areas with cheaper housing place people more easily.
